question: A 60-year-old man with fever and productive cough has dullness to percussion, bronchial breath sounds, and increased vocal resonance over the right lower zone. Which process best explains this combination of signs?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pleural effusion also causes dullness and reduced breath sounds, but bronchial breath sounds and increased vocal resonance are absent — fluid transmits sound poorly.

Correct. Consolidation replaces air with fluid/exudate, transmitting sound better: dullness (reduced air), bronchial breath sounds (solid medium transmits high-frequency tones), and increased vocal resonance (aegophony/whispering pectoriloquy).
Pneumothorax causes hyperresonance (not dullness), absent breath sounds, and decreased vocal resonance due to the air barrier.

Fibrosis causes fine end-inspiratory crackles and reduced lung volumes; it does not cause the classic consolidation triad of dullness + bronchial breathing + increased resonance in an acute febrile illness.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the consolidation signs: solid lung conducts sound — dullness replaces resonance, bronchial sounds replace vesicular, and vocal resonance increases. Contrast this with effusion (dullness but no bronchial sounds, reduced resonance) and pneumothorax (hyperresonance, absent sounds).

Excellent. The triad of dullness + bronchial breath sounds + increased vocal resonance (whispering pectoriloquy, aegophony) is pathognomonic for consolidation and distinguishes it from effusion and pneumothorax on clinical grounds.
